entry.title: The Wolves of Rome
entry.content:
The Capitoline Wolf, Palazzo dei Conservatori, Rome
Source: Author's photo

"The last day is at hand for the Romans...These wolves that made such ravages upon Italian liberty will never vanish until we have cut down the forest that harbours them."

— Velleius Paterculus ii, 27, 21

Few images say “Rome” like the wolf. But the wolf on this denarius of P. Satrienus is not the gentle nurse of Romulus and Remus. She is alone, no twins, no fig tree, no shepherd, and she is on the prowl.

Crawford, the standard catalogue today, calls the head Roma but gives no argument why.2 Grueber, writing for the British Museum sixty years earlier, called it Mars.3 It’s easy to assume the most recent source has settled the debate for all satisfaction. However, when one goes back through the literature you find the older catalogues disagreeing, each for various reasons, and if the latest version simply asserts a position, we are left without an argument for the positon. Working through these reasons yourself exercises the mind and puts any personal conclusion on firmer ground.

Obverse: helmeted head, Mars or Roma?

Reverse: she-wolf walking l.; ROMA above, P SATRIE NVS below

Mars/Roma - Obverse

Grueber’s catalog entry in BMCRR clearly states a young Mars as obverse, but diving into his rich footnotes reveals a deeper conversation. He thinks Mars is more likely because the features look too masculine for a goddess, and notes that Mommsen thought so too4. Babelon looked at the same head and saw long, womanly hair, and seeing the legend ROMA and asserting that ROMA cannot name the wolf, associates Roma as the obverse.5 More recently, Liv Yarrow has come down on Mars too. She argues that an ancient viewer would more naturally have seen Mars, and that he pairs well with the wolf, his sacred animal, on the reverse.6

Resolving this argument is aided by context and deeper reading. Babelon attempts to follow Mommsen, but missed the deeper reading, ROMA names the type, not the design. 7 Reading ROMA as the name of the people who issued the coin has deep roots. Rome’s first silver, the didrachm of the 260s, carries the wolf and twins with ROMANO, “of the Romans,” underneath.8 The first denarii of 211 BCE put ROMA under the galloping Dioscuri for the next century ROMA sits in the exergue below Jupiter, Victory, Luna, and Hercules drawn by centaurs. It is the state’s signature. Then, after about 115 BCE, it fades, and by the Social War it is all but gone.9 By this time the Romans were masters of Italy and no longer needed to say whose coin this was.

Quadrigatus, c. 225–212 BCE (Crawford 28/3): Janiform head of the Dioscuri / Jupiter in a quadriga driven by Victory, ROMA in the exergue
Source: CNG, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.5)

Anonymous denarius, c. 211 BCE (Crawford 44/5): Roma / the Dioscuri galloping r., ROMA in the exergue
Source: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Gallica (public domain)

That’s what makes the legend on this coin stand out. Satrienus is one of the very last moneyers to use ROMA, which is used not to identify the coin to a new audience, but to re-assert Roman mastery of Italy. Reading the coin as a whole: Mars, the god of war, on one obverse; a fierce wolf on the reverse, a dominant Republic steps back up to the mic and says: “Allow me to re-introduce myself.”

Wolf - Reverse

On to the reverse. The wolf has been on Roman coins from the very start. The first Roman silver coins showed a bold Hercules on the obverse she-wolf suckling Romulus and Remus on the reverse. Later, denarii repeated this scene of a protective and nuturing wolf.

Didrachm, c. 269–266 BCE (Crawford 20/1): Hercules / she-wolf suckling the twins, ROMANO
Source: Numismatica Ars Classica, Auction 150 (2 December 2024), lot 730

Anonymous denarius, c. 115–114 BCE (Crawford 287/1): Roma / Roma seated on shields, the she-wolf suckling the twins at her feet, birds on either side
Source: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Gallica (public domain)

Denarius of Sex. Pompeius, 137 BCE (Crawford 235/1): the shepherd Faustulus finds the twins under the fig tree
Source: CNG, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.5)

But our wolf here is not nuturing. There are no twins. She is fierce and described by Crawford as the “Capitoline” wolf.10 Many will take that name to mean the Capitoline Wolf in Musei Capitolini today. Even if the bronze is ancient, and radiocarbon dating suggests it may be medieval,11 it has only been on the Capitol since 1471, and nobody knows where it stood before. There have been various wolves around the city throughout history, and all of them, as far as we can tell, were nursing: the Ogulnii’s wolf and twins at the Ruminal fig tree below the Palatine in 296 BCE12, which Crawford thinks the first didrachm copies;8 a bronze wolf by the fig tree in the Comitium, marking a miracle of the augur Attus Navius;13 and a small gilt group of Romulus at the wolf’s teats that Cicero called the nurse of Roman dominion, struck by lightning in 65 BCE.14

The Wolf is ROMA

Denarius of the Italian rebels under C. Papius Mutilus, c. 90 BCE: Bacchus / the Italian bull goring the Roman wolf
Source: © The Trustees of the British Museum, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

A cleaner reading of the whole coin comes from looking at when it was struck. In 91 BCE Rome’s Italian allies, tired of fighting Rome’s wars without the vote, rebelled.15 The rebels struck their own denarii clearly stating their cause. Under the Samnite general Gaius Papius Mutilus, his name in Oscan below, the bull of Italy gores the Roman wolf to the ground and drives its horn into her.16 This characterization of Rome as ravionus wolves was not isolated only to her former allies. Mithridates of Pontus said the expansionist Romans has the “disposition of wolves” and instatiable for blood, tyranny, and riches. 17

In word and in metal, Rome was a wolf, and not a motherly one.

Footnotes

  1. “… adiiciens numquam defuturos raptores Italicae libertatis lupos, nisi silva, in quam refugere solerent, esset excisa.” (adding: “These wolves that made such ravages upon Italian liberty will never vanish until we have cut down the forest that harbours them.”) -Velleius Paterculus ii, 27, 1–3 (tr. F. W. Shipley). ↩

  2. Crawford describes the type as, “Helmeted head of Roma r.; behind, control-mark. Border of dots. / She-wolf l.; above, ROMA; in exergue, P·SATRIENVS. Border of dots.” -M. H. Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974), I, p. 403, no. 388/1b ↩

  3. Grueber describes the type as, “Head of young Mars r., wearing crested helmet. / P·SATRIE NVS (in exergue). Wolf walking l.; above, ROMA.” -H. A. Grueber, Coins of the Roman Republic in the British Museum (1910), I, p. 392, no. 3208, Pl. xlii. 6 ↩

  4. “This head may be of Mars or Roma, but more probably of the former, as the features are too masculine for the female divinity. This was also Mommsen’s opinion (Hist. mon. rom., t. ii., p. 479), but Babelon (vol. ii., p. 420) gives reasons for identifying the head as that of Roma. As Mars was the father of Romulus and Remus, either would be applicable in point of connection with the reverse type, in which may be seen a reference to the foundation of Rome.” -H. A. Grueber, Coins of the Roman Republic in the British Museum (1910), I, pp. 392–393, no. 3208 and n. 3. ↩

  5. “La tête casquée qui figure au droit est celle de la déesse Rome, plutôt que celle de Mars ; elle a de très longs cheveux comme une femme, et la légende Roma du revers paraît s’y rapporter. A cette époque, en effet, le nom de Rome sur les deniers, quand il paraît, ne sert plus qu’à l’indication du type, et l’on n’a jamais donné le nom de Roma à la louve.” (The helmeted head on the obverse is that of the goddess Roma rather than Mars. It has very long hair like a woman’s, and the legend ROMA on the reverse seems to refer to it. At this period, in fact, the name of Rome on denarii, when it appears, serves only to indicate the type, and the name Roma was never given to the she-wolf.) -E. Babelon, Description historique et chronologique des monnaies de la République romaine (1886), II, pp. 420–421, Satriena 1. ↩

  6. L. M. Yarrow, “Mars, not Roma” (5 July 2021). Yarrow’s starting point is a helmeted statuette from Lombardy now in the Louvre. She returns to the question in two later posts, “More on Mars (not Roma) on obverses” (2022) and “Mars, not Roma (again)” (2022). ↩

  7. “Helmeted head of Mars. R/ She-wolf walking. Above it is the word ROMA, which should be taken as an explanatory legend. However, the name Roma was never given to the she-wolf” (citing A. Schwegler, Römische Geschichte I, p. 423). On the legend in general: “From the year 670 [84 BCE] onward it serves only to indicate the type: for example, on some denarii of T. Carisius and of Cato of Utica, in the Caesarian period, and on no. 265 [Satrienus].” -Th. Mommsen, Histoire de la monnaie romaine, tr. Blacas (1870), II, pp. 479 and 166 (Claude’s translation from the French). ↩

  8. “With the beginning of silver coinage at Rome itself in 269–268, at least one distinctively Roman type appears, the wolf and twins on the reverse of the didrachm, copying the statue set up in 296 by Cn. Ogulnius and Q. Ogulnius.” -M. H. Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage II, p. 714. See RRC 20/1. ↩ ↩2

  9. By my count, about 220 denarius types in Crawford’s catalogue carry ROMA. From 211 BCE it sits on the reverse under the Dioscuri and later under nearly every chariot type, on coins whose obverse is Roma, Mars (Crawford 234/1, 296/1), Sol or Saturn. After about 106 BCE it turns up beside heads of Apollo, Diana and Hercules, and from 81 BCE it is “extremely rare”: Crawford counts Satrienus (on the reverse, “with the Capitoline wolf”) and three obverse uses (Poblicius, Cato, Carisius). Crawford himself reads ROMA beside the helmeted female head (136–108 BCE) as identifying her as Roma. On Satrienus, though, it sits on the other side of the coin. -M. H. Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage II, pp. 723–724. ↩

  10. “The moneyer is a P. Satrienus, not otherwise known … For the she-wolf of the Capitol, apparently portrayed here, see W. Helbig, Führer ii⁴, 277; E. Gjerstad, Early Rome iv, 492; this type of ferocious wolf has no original connection with the wolf that nursed Romulus and Remus (for which see p. 714), but was perhaps adopted as a symbol of Rome after the defeat of those rebel Italians who likened Rome to a predatory wolf (so E. J. Bickerman, RFIC 1969, 395-6); if this is right, the type is perhaps anti-Italian in intention.” -M. H. Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974), I, pp. 403–404, RRC 388/1b. Crawford dates the issue to 77 BCE (pp. 82–84). ↩

  11. Capitoline Wolf, Wikipedia, which summarizes the dating dispute. Crawford’s two references, Helbig’s guide to the Roman museums and Gjerstad’s Early Rome, both come from the 1960s, before the scientific dating. ↩

  12. “In that same year Gnaeus and Quintus Ogulnius the curule aediles brought a number of usurers to trial, and, confiscating their possessions, employed the share which came into the public treasury to put brazen thresholds in the Capitol … and at the fig-tree Ruminalis a representation of the infant Founders of the City being suckled by the wolf.” -Livy x, 23, 11–12 (tr. B. O. Foster, Loeb 1926, pp. 444–445) ↩

  13. Pliny, Natural History xv, 20 (77), on the sacred fig in the Forum and Comitium: the fig was honoured “quoniam sub ea inventa est lupa infantibus praebens rumim” (because under it the she-wolf was found offering her teat to the infants), In Bostock and Riley’s translation: “A group in bronze was afterwards erected to consecrate the remembrance of this miraculous event, as, through the agency of Attus Navius the augur, the tree itself had passed spontaneously from its original locality to the Comitium in the Forum.” -Pliny, NH xv, 20 (tr. J. Bostock and H. T. Riley, 1855). Wikipedia gives the Ogulnii’s statue as 295 BC; Foster’s Livy puts that chapter in 296. ↩

  14. “Even Romulus, who built this city, was struck, which, you recollect, stood in the Capitol, a gilt statue, little and sucking, and clinging to the teats of the wolf.” -Cicero, In Catilinam iii, 19 (Latin text linked; tr. C. D. Yonge, 1856). In his poem on his consulship Cicero calls her “Martia … Romani nominis altrix”, “the Martian beast, the nurse of Roman dominion,” De Divinatione i, 20 (tr. W. A. Falconer). ↩

  15. “The fortune of the Italians was as cruel as their cause was just; for they were seeking citizenship in the state whose power they were defending by their arms; every year and in every war they were furnishing a double number of men, both of cavalry and of infantry, and yet were not admitted to the rights of citizens in the state which, through their efforts, had reached so high a position that it could look down upon men of the same race and blood as foreigners and aliens.” -Velleius Paterculus ii, 15, 2 (tr. F. W. Shipley) ↩

  16. “The allegorical allusion of this type is so very evident that any comment would be superfluous. It is the bull, the emblem or symbol of Italy and the Samnite nation, overcoming the she-wolf, the emblem of Rome.” -H. A. Grueber, Coins of the Roman Republic in the British Museum (1910), II, p. 327 n. 2; See also A. Sambon, Les monnaies antiques de l’Italie (1903), nos. 222–226. ↩

  17. “That they had made it a law to themselves to hate all kings … and as their founders, according to their report, were suckled by the teats of a wolf, so the whole race had the disposition of wolves, being insatiable of blood and tyranny, and eager and hungry after riches.” -Justin xxxviii, 6, 7–8 (tr. J. S. Watson) ↩
entry.summary: From the she-wolf of the foundation myth to the men Rome called wolves, a look at the animal on Republican coins.

entry.title: Who Is on the Statue? The Aqua Marcia Denarius

link.title: Who Is on the Statue? The Aqua Marcia Denarius

entry.content:
The Aqua Marcia aqueduct
Source: Wikimedia Commons

The first to begin the bringing of this water to Rome was one of the kings, Ancus Marcius ; later, repairs were carried out by Quintus Marcius Rex in his praetorship, and again by Marcus Agrippa.

— Pliny, Natural History, Book 31, Chapter 24

But we must go on to describe marvels which are unsurpassed in virtue of their genuine value. Quintus Marcius Rex, having been ordered by the senate to repair the conduits of the day Aqua Appia, the Anio, and the Tepula, drove underground passages through the mountains and brought to Rome a new water-supply called by his own name and completed within the period of his praetorship.

- Pliny, Natural History Book 36, Chapter 121

Ancient Kings and Aquaducts

Ancient coins can provide clear messages for their meaning and at other times the story they wish to tell is rather opaque. Take the obverse of this coin. A noble diademed bust with ANCVS written behind is a clear indication the obverse represents the mythical fourth king of Rome, Ancus Marcius. The reverse dramatically shows an aqueduct with the letters AQVA MAR below clearly spelling out to the viewer this is the Aqua Marcia built by the praetor Q. Marcius Rex between 144-140 BCE1. The moneyer, L. Marcius Philippus, is using this miniature monument to celebrate the Marcii gens through the connection to Rome’s king and the aqueduct2. The connection is meaningful as Ancus was reported to be the first to bring water to the city via aqueduct3. However, the identity and purpose of the equestrian statue is a bit muddled- who is that statue and why is it on top of an aqueduct?

Use of Imagery and Identification

First, let’s disabuse ourselves of the requirement that the reverse depicts a true to life scene. Roman moneyers often invoked mythical imagery, ancient heroes, pulled from various distant family branches, or depicted buildings not yet finished to convey meaning4. Furthermore, a statue on top of an aqueduct is both an engineering impossibility and a political waste5. The aqueduct was buried on its route to the Capitoline and so any standing equestrian statue would be far from the city and the viewing populace with little political value. Consequently, Grueber’s claim that “In commemoration of the great benefit derived from this new water supply the Senate placed an equestrian statue of Marcius on the aqueduct” 6 is unsupported in fact and in practice.

So if there wasn’t an enormous statue on an aqueduct, who/what was intended for the audience to recall? We have seen Grueber’s claim to be it being of Q. Marcius Rex, but Crawford is more circumspect stating clearly “The statue is problematical” 7 and simply summarizing it as “equestrian”. This missing piece of this puzzle is not textual, but archaeological. Both Crawford and Mommsen8 point to a military diploma from a discharge legionary found far from the Captioline Hill to help reveal the statue’s identity. Stunningly, that find was preserved and is available electronically to read:

ROMAE • IN • CAPITOLIO • POST • AEDEM • IOVIS • O . M . IN BASI • Q • MARCI • REGIS PR

Which translates as: “At Rome, on the Capitoline behind the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximums on the pedestal [of the statue] of Q. Marcius Rex praetor” 9.

Military diploma upper portion

Military diploma lower portion

Military diploma of Gaius Pontius, CIL XVI, 5. Source: Wikimedia Commons

Upon their discharge, legionaries were often granted citizen and a land allotment. This grant of citizenship was publically recorded, so that in theory, their rights could be verified. This diploma from the late Republic was found in Illyria and was likely the soldier’s personal copy, with the “official” copy attached to the statue of Q. Marcius Rex, that existed on the Capitoline Hill.

Conclusion or New Directions?

So that’s it? The status is Q. Marcius Rex through hard archaeological evidence now. Well, new scholarship by Dr. Liv Yarrow in “The Roman Republic to 49BCE: Using Coins as Sources” has begun to turn this understanding on its head. Yarrow, building on the work by Hölkeskamp, argues that the statue is of Q. Marcius Tremulus (cos. 306), who was a hero of the early Republic for twice defeating the Samnites and then the Anagni. The key to identifying Tremulus is the depiction of the rider as wearing a toga, rather than military garb. In a brief description of the statue, Pliny specifically calls out this distinction:

Also there was in front of the temple of the Castors an equestrian statue of Quintus Marcius Tremulus, wearing a toga ; he had twice vanquished the Samnites, and by taking Anagni -Pliny, Natural History 34:23

The Temple of Castor and Pollux is at the heart of the Forum and the statue of Tremulus would be visible and recognizable to any Roman citizen. Yarrow argues that the use of Tremulus’ statue, paired with the Aqua Marcia, is an attempt to re-appropriate the massive project for the Marcii Philippi (the gens to which our moneyer belongs) and away from the Marcii Reges (the gens of its builder, Q. Marcius Rex). Tremelus is also a repeated figure on coins of the Marcii Philippi, all as a rider on horseback. Furthermore, the design itself may have been in contest with similar claims of the Aemili Lepidii over the “ownership” of the aquaduct who earlier issued coins showing an equestrian rider over top an unnamed aquaduct10. I find myself wanting to agree with Yarrow but wishing to dive into these other Marcii coins to truly see the connection to Tremulus11.

Reverse of our denarius of L. Marcius Philippus

Competing claims to the aqua Marcia by Mn. Aemilius Lepidus (CRR 293/1) Source: ANS 1941.131.97

Denarius of Q. Marcius Philippus (Crawford 259/1) issued in 129 BCE showing Tremelus on horseback. Source ANS 1963.31.39

Denarius of L. Marcius Philippus (Crawford 293/1) issued in 113/112 BCE. Source ANS 1992.41.10

The Joys of the Late Republic

This long tortured story about the simple question of “who is on the statue?” is why I love late Republican coinage. These small objects are steeped in myth, memory, and politics. For a hobby, it provides the ability to examine beautiful objects, dive into historical books, and weigh arguments of academic titans. It’s quite a fun and lengthy journey.

References and Footnotes

  1. “The Senate commissioned Marcius, who at that time administered the law as praetor between citizens, to reclaim and repair these conduits; and since the growth of the City was seen to demand a more bountiful supply of water, the same man was charged by the Senate to bring into the City other waters so far as he cloud”. -Frontius De Aquaducts I, 7 ↩

  2. “Several decades later, in 56 BCE, on the obverse of the coinage of a certain Philippus, one finds Ancus Marcius again, alone this time, wearing a crown and with a lituus behind him. In this way, the moneyer, who can probably be identified as L. Marcius Philippus, son of the consul of the same name in that year and himself consul suffectus in 38 bce, alludes to the augurate of his like-named grandfather, who was consul in 91 BCE and censor in 86 BCE” -Karl-J Hölkeskamp, ‘In the Web of (Hi-)Stories: Memoria, Monuments, and Their Myth-Historical ‘Interconnectedness’’, in Karl Galinsky (ed.), Memory in Ancient Rome and Early Christianity ↩

  3. “The first to begin the bringing of this water to Rome was one of the kings, Ancus Marcius; later, repairs were carried out by Quintus Marcius Rex in his praetorship, and again by Marcus Agrippa.” -Pliny, Natural History, Book 31, Chapter 24 ↩

  4. “In the more widely-spread medium of coinage, even greater liberties were taken, and the multilayered ambiguous images and complex combinations of motifs and symbols in the coinage of the late Republic document this trend. It was common practice for the tresviri monetales in charge of issuing coinage, mostly young men at the beginning of their careers, not only to adopt familial, symbolic capital in a strict sense, but also to include well-known achievements of their ancestors from other branches of their gens in their own account and even to suggest bold, even fantastical genealogical combinations, which did not have any place in the Republican family tree (e.g. not in the official imagines of the ancestors in the atrium and mutatis mutandis in the pompa funebris), such as the descent of the gens from mythical characters, gods, demigods, and heroes” -Karl-J Hölkeskamp, ‘In the Web of (Hi-)Stories: Memoria, Monuments, and Their Myth-Historical ‘Interconnectedness’’, in Karl Galinsky (ed.), Memory in Ancient Rome and Early Christianity ↩

  5. “Moreover, no one would wish to assert that the statue was actually superimposed upon the arches of the aqueduct—that would be utterly ridiculous; nor could the arches have been situated on the Capitol, where subterranean tunneling—rather than arched construction—was required.” - Translation from Orelli-Henzen, n° 5088, 6838. - Bullet, de l’lust, arch., 1845, р. 121 ↩

  6. BMCRR Rome p. 486; To support this statement Gruber cites Mommsen’s description of the coin in Histoire de la monnaie romaine Volume II p. 513. However, Mommsen simply calls the statue equestrian, but in a footnote, indicates that is probably Q. Marcius Rex citing an inscription from a military diploma which will be crucial later in our discussion. ↩

  7. Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage, p. 449. ↩

  8. Crawford references (CIL xvi, 5), while Mommesen deep in Histoire de la monnaie romaine Volume II p. 513 (footnote 4) points to Orelli-Henzen, n° 5088, 6838. - Bullet, de l’lust, arch., 1845, р. 121 ↩

  9. I am thankful for Dr. Eva Carrara for this translation and finding the sources for this diploma. ↩

  10. Denarius of Mn. Aemilius Lepidus, Crawford 291/1 ↩

  11. More evidence to follow on her post 1 and post 2 ↩
entry.summary: A denarius shows an equestrian statue atop an aqueduct. Identifying the rider takes a military diploma, Pliny, and a new reading by Liv Yarrow.

entry.title: Pompey the Great: Three Triumphs and the Road to Pharsalus

link.title: Pompey the Great: Three Triumphs and the Road to Pharsalus

entry.content:
Bust of Pompey the Great
Source: Wikimedia Commons

He [Pompey] celebrated the triumph in honour of all his wars at once, including in it many trophies beauti­fully decked out to represent each of his achievements, even the smallest; and after them all came one huge one, decked out in costly fashion and bearing an inscription stating that it was a trophy of the inhabited world ... These [honors] consisted in the privilege of always wearing the laurel wreath at all public games, and arraying himself in the cloak of a general at all of them, as well as in the triumphal garb at the horse-races. They had been granted him chiefly through the cooperation of Caesar, and contrary to the advice of Marcus Cato.

— Cassius Dio xxxvii, 21, 2 and 4

This coin was issued by Faustus Cornelius Sulla, son of the Dictator Sulla, and highlights the achievements of his father-in-law, Cnaius Pompey, known to us as Pompey the Great. The obverse shows young Hercules mirroring Alexander the Great’s coinage and symbolizing Pompey’s swift rise. The reverse displays his three triumphs1 across the known world in Europe, Africa, and Asia (three small wreaths), a boat stern (aplustre) for clearing the Mediterranean of pirates2, an ear of corn for securing Rome’s grain supply3, and the unprecedented honor of a golden triumphal crown.4 These symbols encircle a globe, reflecting Cicero’s claim that through Pompey and these three triumphs, we “witness the whole world being under our rule.”5

Sulla’s Civil War

While Pompey wasn’t born “great,” he had a gift for timing and for choosing the winning side. He served with his father during the Social War, but his rise began in 83 BCE when, at just twenty‑three, he joined Sulla’s campaign. Raising his own legions and defeating Sulla’s enemies in Sicily and Africa, he sought a triumph — or so he thought. Sulla refused until Pompey hinted that “more worship the rising than the setting sun”.6 First triumph secured, then hubris followed: he tried to enter the city in an elephant‑drawn chariot, but the gate was too narrow.7

Typical obverse design for Alexander's coinage showing the head of Hercules wearing the skin of the Nemean lion
Source: Madison Art Collection

Golden corona wreath worn by triumphators
Source: Author's photo of Brooklyn Museum "Wreath"

Sertorius’ Rebellion

Pompey continued to serve the Sullan cause after the Dictator’s death. He was appointed proconsul to deal with the Marian rebel Sertorius’ rebellion in Spain in 76 BCE. After several years the rebellion was put down, and Pompey returned to Italy just in time to intercept the remnants of Spartacus’ army, stealing Crassus’ glory in the Third Servile War.8 Seizing the moment, Pompey and Crassus sought election as consuls. Neither dismissed his army: Pompey claimed he was waiting for his triumph, and Crassus insisted he would not do so until Pompey.9 Both were elected consul and Pompey acquired his second triumph.

Cilician Pirates and the Third Mithridatic War

In the subsequent years, Pompey continued to be relied on by the state to solve crises, and also inserted himself into adventures for further glory. In 67 BCE Pompey was granted an extraordinary command to deal with the issue of piracy in the Mediterranean. Granted proconsular power in any province within 50 miles of the Mediterranean and the power to appoint legates in his name2, he was Augustus in all but name forty years before his time. While he ended the threat of piracy rapidly, in under three months, he then leveraged this opportunity to undermine Lucullus and take over his command in the Third Mithridatic War10,11. Seizing a war nearly won, Pompey made unreasonable surrender conditions on Mithridates to force a decisive series of battles. During this time, Pompey extended the Asian province and annexed new ones including Cilicia, Bithynia and Pontus, and Syria, extending Roman control to the entire Mediterranean seaboard which was truly “Mare Nostrum” (Our Sea).

The Road to Pharsalus

Third triumph achieved but the seeds of Pompey’s downfall, and eventually that of the Republic, were finally sown. Upon returning to Rome, the Senate, fearful of Pompey’s rising power, refused to ratify his reorganization of the eastern provinces or settlements for his veterans. With no further recourse, Pompey aligned with Crassus and Caesar to achieve his aims through the First Triumvirate.

The Republic could not withstand the power of these three towering individuals, and in the end, neither could they withstand each other. Crassus would die in an ill-fated adventure in Parthia, and with the death of Pompey’s beloved wife Julia, the alliance with Caesar would fully collapse — as Lucan observed, Pompey could bear no rival and Caesar no equal.12 By 49 BCE, Caesar and Pompey were opposing sides of the latest Roman civil war. The constant obstinacy of the Optimates created a conflict that neither wanted, and eventually their endless pressure forced Pompey into a battle at Pharsalus that he did not want. Pompey the Great would finally lose this battl, and then eventually his life, betrayed by Ptolemy XIII (a former client) on the banks of the Nile.

Footnotes

  1. “These triumphs were: (1) on his victory in Africa over a Marian refugee Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus and a Numidian leader Iarbas, celebrated on 12 March 79 (or 80) b.c.; (2) “ex Hispaniis,” on the last day of 71 b.c., after the Sertorian War; (3) over the pirates and Mithridates, on 28 and 29 September 61 b.c.” -Loeb Classic Library, Cicero Balbo 16, Footnote B ↩

  2. Under the lex Gabinia, Pompey cleared the Mediterranean of pirates in 67 BCE. See Plutarch, Pompey 25 and Cassius Dio, Roman History 36.23–24. ↩ ↩2

  3. Pompey was elected Praefectus Annonae in 57 BCE. And when Cicero returned to the city⁠ by virtue of the law then passed, he immediately reconciled Pompey to the senate, and by his advocacy of the corn law he in a manner once more made Pompey master of all the land and sea in Roman possession. For under his direction were placed harbours, trading-places, distributions of crops, — in a word, navigation and agriculture.⁠ … Having thus been set over the administration and management of the grain trade, Pompey sent out his agents and friends in various directions, while he himself sailed to Sicily, Sardinia and Africa, and collected grain. -Plutarch, Pompey 49 - 50 ↩

  4. Granted in 63 BCE. “In Pompey’s absence the tribunes of the people, Titus Ampius and Titus Labienus, proposed a law that at the games of the circus Pompey should be permitted to wear a golden crown and the full dress of the triumphator, and at the theatre the purple-bordered toga and the golden crown.” -Velleius Paterculus ii, 40, 4: ↩

  5. “For if Pompeius had lived five hundred years ago ; if this man, from whom, while yet a mere youth and a Roman knight, the senate had frequently sought aid for the common safety, whose exploits, attended always with the most glorious victory on sea and land, had extended through all nations, whose three triumphs proved that the whole world was subject to our sway, whom the Roman people had distinguished with unprecedented and singular honours..” - Cicero, Balbo 16 ↩

  6. “After this, Pompey asked for a triumph, but Sulla opposed his request …. Pompey, however, was not cowed, but bade Sulla reflect that more worshipped the rising than the setting sun, intimating that his own power was on the increase, while that of Sulla was on the wane and fading away. Sulla did not hear the words distinctly, but seeing, from their looks and gestures, that those who did hear them were amazed, he asked what it was that had been said. When he learned what it was, he was astounded at the boldness of Pompey, and cried out twice in succession: “Let him triumph!” -Plutarch, Pompey 14.1-3 ↩

  7. “Further, when many showed displeasure and indignation at his project, Pompey, we are told, was all the more desirous of annoying them, and tried to ride into the city on a chariot drawn by four elephants; for he had brought many from Africa which he had captured from its kings. But the gate of the city was too narrow, and he therefore gave up the attempt and changed over to his horses” -Plutarch, Pompey 14.4 ↩

  8. “…But although Crassus had been fortunate, had shown most excellent general­ship, and had exposed his person to danger, nevertheless, his success did not fail to enhance the reputation of Pompey. For the fugitives from the battle⁠ encountered that general and were cut to pieces, so he could write to the senate that in open battle, indeed, Crassus had conquered the slaves, but that he himself had extirpated the war.” Plutarch, Crassus 11.7 ↩

  9. “Crassus accomplished his task within six months, whence arose a contention for honours between himself and Pompey. Crassus did not dismiss his army, for Pompey did not dismiss his. Both were candidates for the consul­ship. Crassus had been praetor as the law of Sulla required. Pompey had been neither praetor nor quaestor, and was only thirty-four years old, but he had promised the tribunes of the people that much of their former power should be restored. When they were chosen consuls they did not even then dismiss their armies, which were stationed near the city. Each one offered an excuse. Pompey said that he was waiting the return of Metellus for his Spanish triumph; Crassus said that Pompey ought to dismiss his army first.” -Appian, Civil Wars Book 1, 121 ↩

  10. “The rest of the soldiers Pompey summoned by letter, for he had already been appointed to conduct the war against Mithridates and Tigranes, because he won the favour of the people and flattered their leaders. But the Senate and the nobility considered Lucullus a wronged man. He had been superseded, they said, not in a war, but in a triumph, and had been forced to relinquish and turn over to others, not his campaign, but the prizes of victory in his campaign”. -Plutarch, Lucullus 35.7 ↩

  11. On the passage of the lex Manilia and Pompey’s assumption of the eastern command over Mithridates and Tigranes, see Plutarch, Pompey 30–31. ↩

  12. “nec coisse pares. erat plus ferre nec ulla Pompeius” (They could not meet as equals; Pompey could endure no superior, and Caesar no equal). Lucan, Pharsalia Book I, lines 125–126. ↩
entry.summary: Pompey's rise from Sulla's lieutenant to the first man of Rome, told through the symbols on a denarius struck by Sulla's son.
